walkthroughs.body_html:
Paper 2: Dimensions of Linguistic Variation — a core area of A-Level English Language.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Paper 2: Dimensions of Linguistic Variation brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Paper 2: Dimensions of Linguistic Variation.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: How many phonemes in standard English?
What does Labov's research show about language variation?
options: Labov showed that everyone speaks the same way regardless of background.
Labov showed that working-class people speak ungrammatically.
Language varies systematically by social class, gender, age and context — and speakers shift style depending on formality, often unconsciously.
A dialect is a foreign language; an accent is how locals speak.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between a dialect and an accent?
options: Accent refers only to pronunciation; dialect includes vocabulary and grammar as well as pronunciation — so all dialects involve accents but not vice versa.
Both terms mean the same — analysing language scientifically.
A dialect is a foreign language; an accent is how locals speak.
Dialect and accent mean the same thing.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between descriptive and prescriptive approaches to language?
options: Both terms mean the same — analysing language scientifically.
Descriptivists describe how language is actually used; prescriptivists rule on how language ought to be used — modern linguistics is descriptivist.
Descriptivists describe written language and prescriptivists describe spoken language.
A dialect is a foreign language; an accent is how locals speak.
